_about: Your energy glossary. Add, edit or remove entries freely. level: 1 basics, 2 intermediate, 3 expert. category: nuclear | markets | transition | tech. Edits made in the app are stored on your phone; use Export there to copy them back into this file.

terms.definition: A reactor of up to roughly 300 MWe per unit, designed so major parts are built in a factory and shipped, aiming for lower upfront cost and faster construction than large plants.
A very small reactor (typically under ~20 MWe) that can be transported largely whole, intended for remote sites, military bases, data centers or industrial heat.
Evolutionary light-water reactor designs (e.g. AP1000, EPR, APR1400) with improved passive safety, longer design life and standardized licensing compared with earlier plants.

Advanced reactor families that move away from conventional water cooling: sodium- and lead-cooled fast reactors, molten salt, high-temperature gas and supercritical water reactors. Goals include higher temperatures, better fuel use and less long-lived waste.
The dominant reactor type worldwide, using ordinary water as both coolant and moderator. Includes PWRs and BWRs.
An LWR where water is kept under high pressure so it doesn't boil in the core; heat passes to a secondary loop that makes steam. Gösgen is a Swiss example.
An LWR where water boils directly in the core and the steam drives the turbine. Leibstadt is a Swiss example.
A reactor without a moderator, so fission is driven by high-energy neutrons. It can breed new fuel and burn long-lived actinides, usually cooled by sodium, lead or molten salt.
A reactor using molten fluoride or chloride salt as coolant, and sometimes with fuel dissolved in the salt. Operates at low pressure and high temperature.
A helium-cooled, graphite-moderated reactor reaching outlet temperatures around 750°C or more, useful for industrial heat and hydrogen. Usually fuelled with TRISO particles.
Tiny uranium kernels coated in layers of carbon and silicon carbide that retain fission products even at very high temperatures. Used in HTGRs and several microreactors.
Uranium enriched to between 5% and 20% U-235. Many advanced reactors need it; commercial supply outside Russia is still being built up.
Raising the share of fissile U-235 above its natural 0.7%. Most power reactors use 3–5%.
The standard measure of the effort needed to enrich uranium; enrichment services are priced per SWU.
The chain from uranium mining, conversion, enrichment and fuel fabrication through reactor use to storage, reprocessing or disposal of spent fuel.
How much energy has been extracted from fuel, usually in GWd per tonne of heavy metal. Higher burnup means more energy per tonne and less spent fuel volume.
Fuel made from a blend of plutonium and uranium oxides, typically using plutonium recovered by reprocessing.
Chemically separating usable uranium and plutonium from spent fuel. Practiced in France; Switzerland's 2018 energy law ended reprocessing of Swiss spent fuel.
Fuel removed from a reactor after use. Highly radioactive and hot; stored in pools, then dry casks, pending reprocessing or deep geological disposal.
Permanent disposal of high-level waste hundreds of meters underground in stable rock. Finland's Onkalo is the first; Switzerland's Nagra proposed Nördlich Lägern as its site.
Heavy elements like neptunium, americium and curium formed in reactors. They dominate the long-term radiotoxicity of spent fuel; fast reactors and accelerator-driven systems can transmute them.
Converting long-lived radioactive isotopes into shorter-lived or stable ones by neutron irradiation, to shrink the waste burden.
A subcritical reactor kept running by neutrons from a particle accelerator; switching off the beam stops the reaction. Studied for waste transmutation.
Safety functions that rely on physics (gravity, natural circulation, convection) rather than pumps, power or operator action to cool the reactor in an emergency.
Actual energy produced over a period divided by what the plant would produce at full power all the time. Nuclear typically runs 85–93%, solar 10–25%, onshore wind 25–40%.
Thorium-232 is not fissile but can be converted into fissile U-233 in a reactor. More abundant than uranium; used in some MSR and HWR concepts.
A reactor that produces more fissile material than it consumes, usually a fast reactor turning U-238 into plutonium.

Joining light nuclei (usually deuterium and tritium) to release energy. Main approaches are magnetic confinement (tokamaks, stellarators) and inertial confinement (lasers). Not yet producing net electricity.
A doughnut-shaped device confining plasma with magnetic fields and a current driven in the plasma. ITER and SPARC are tokamaks.
A fusion device using twisted external magnets to confine plasma without a large plasma current, allowing steady-state operation. Wendelstein 7-X is the leading example.
Fusion power out divided by heating power put into the plasma. Q > 1 is scientific breakeven; a power plant needs much higher Q plus efficient conversion to electricity.

Running existing reactors beyond their original design life (often 40 → 60 or 80 years) after safety reviews and upgrades. Switzerland has no fixed operating limit; plants run as long as ENSI deems them safe.
Shutting down, decontaminating and dismantling a nuclear plant. Mühleberg (shut down 2019) is Switzerland's first.
The average lifetime cost per MWh of building and running a plant. Useful for rough comparison, but ignores system costs like backup, storage and grid.
The blended cost of a project's debt and equity. For capital-heavy nuclear projects, financing cost is often the biggest driver of LCOE.
Costs beyond the plant itself: grid connection, balancing, backup capacity and storage needed to integrate a technology into the power system.
Ranking power plants by marginal cost; the cheapest run first, and the last plant needed to meet demand sets the market price.
In most European power markets every producer receives the price of the most expensive unit needed, which is why gas prices often set electricity prices.
The minimum level of demand over a day, and plants that run continuously to cover it. Also a product traded in power markets (constant delivery 24/7).
Generation that can be turned up or down on demand (gas, hydro, nuclear to a degree), as opposed to weather-dependent wind and solar.
The highest demand periods, and the delivery product covering weekday daytime hours.
A mechanism paying plants for being available to generate when needed, not just for energy delivered, to secure supply in tight hours.
A long-term contract to buy electricity from a specific generator at agreed terms. Tech companies increasingly sign PPAs with nuclear plants and developers.
A contract guaranteeing a strike price: when the market is below it the generator is topped up, when above it pays back. Used in the UK for Hinkley Point C and offshore wind.
Hours when generators pay to deliver power, typically when high solar or wind output meets low demand and inflexible plants can't ramp down.
Short-term power trading: the day-ahead auction sets hourly (now 15-minute in Europe) prices for tomorrow; intraday trading adjusts closer to delivery.
Trading electricity for delivery months or years ahead, used by utilities and large consumers to hedge price risk (e.g. on EEX).
A cap-and-trade market where emitters must hold allowances for each tonne of CO₂. The EU ETS is linked with the Swiss ETS.
A cost on CO₂ emissions, via a tax or an ETS, making fossil generation more expensive relative to low-carbon sources.
Balancing remaining greenhouse gas emissions with removals so net emissions are zero. Switzerland's legal target is 2050.
Reducing the CO₂ intensity of an economy or sector, e.g. by replacing fossil power with nuclear and renewables.
Switching end uses like heating, transport and industry from fossil fuels to electricity, which raises total power demand.
The weather-driven, partly predictable fluctuation of wind and solar output.
Deliberately reducing renewable output because the grid can't absorb or transport it.
The stabilizing effect of large spinning turbines on grid frequency. Inverter-based solar and wind provide little unless grid-forming inverters are used.
Services that keep grid frequency at 50 Hz by adding or removing power within seconds to minutes; procured by TSOs like Swissgrid.
The company running the high-voltage grid and keeping supply and demand balanced. Swissgrid in Switzerland.
When transmission lines can't carry all the power that markets want to move, forcing redispatch and creating price differences between zones.
Shifting energy in time: batteries (hours), pumped hydro (hours to days, big in Switzerland), and hydrogen or seasonal storage (weeks to months).
Grid-scale batteries, usually lithium-ion, used for short-duration shifting and frequency services.
Pumping water uphill when power is cheap and releasing it through turbines when needed. Nant de Drance in Valais is a large Swiss example.
Switzerland's structural shortfall of domestic electricity in winter, when solar is low and demand high, currently covered by imports.
Shorthand for how hydrogen is made: green (renewable electrolysis), pink/purple (nuclear-powered electrolysis), blue (gas with carbon capture), grey (gas without capture).
Splitting water into hydrogen and oxygen with electricity. High-temperature electrolysis can use reactor heat to improve efficiency.
A device moving heat from outside air or ground into buildings, delivering 3–4 units of heat per unit of electricity.
Capturing CO₂ from plants or industry and storing it underground.
An inverter that sets voltage and frequency itself, like a synchronous generator, helping stabilize grids with high shares of solar, wind and batteries.

IEA scenario that includes policies already in force plus those governments have announced and are judged likely to implement. Not a forecast, but the most-cited 'where we're heading' case; ~2.5 °C by 2100 in WEO 2025.
IEA scenario that assumes only policies already in force today, with no new ones. Reintroduced in WEO 2025; ~2.9 °C by 2100. Acts as a floor for ambition.
IEA normative scenario that reaches net-zero energy CO₂ by 2050, consistent with ~1.5 °C after a small overshoot. Shows what would be required, not what is expected.
A scenario that asks 'what happens if…?' — e.g. current policies continue or costs keep falling — and lets the outcome (emissions, warming) emerge. Contrast with a normative scenario.

A scenario that starts from a target (e.g. net zero by 2050, 1.5 °C) and works backwards to find a pathway that meets it. It shows what is needed, not what is likely. Also called a back-casting scenario.

A model that links the energy system, economy, land use and climate in one framework (e.g. MESSAGE, REMIND, IMAGE, GCAM). The IPCC's mitigation pathways come from IAMs. Broad in scope but coarse in time and space.

A bottom-up model that finds the least-cost mix of technologies to meet energy demand under constraints such as a CO₂ cap (e.g. TIMES, OSeMOSYS, PyPSA). Rich in technology detail; its 'optimal' answer is sensitive to cost assumptions.

When global warming temporarily exceeds a target such as 1.5 °C and is later brought back down, which requires net-negative emissions (CO₂ removal). Most remaining 1.5 °C pathways now involve overshoot.

The total amount of CO₂ that can still be emitted while keeping warming below a given level with a given probability. Because warming tracks cumulative CO₂, what matters is the total, not the emission rate in any single year.

Activities that take CO₂ out of the atmosphere and store it durably — afforestation, BECCS, direct air capture, enhanced weathering. Different from CCS, which only stops new emissions from a point source.

terms.full: Bioenergy with Carbon Capture and Storage
terms.definition: Burning or converting biomass for energy and capturing and storing the CO₂. Because plants absorbed that CO₂ while growing, it can give net-negative emissions. Heavily used in IAM pathways, but limited by land, water and biodiversity.
Machines that pull CO₂ directly from ambient air using chemical sorbents, for storage or use. Energy-hungry and currently expensive (hundreds of USD per tonne).
A country's climate pledge under the Paris Agreement, updated every five years. UNEP estimates full implementation of current NDCs leads to ~2.3–2.5 °C of warming.
How IPCC AR6 groups model pathways by warming outcome: C1 = 1.5 °C with no or limited overshoot, C2 = 1.5 °C after high overshoot, C3 = likely below 2 °C, C4 = below 2 °C, up to C8 = above 4 °C.
Five storylines (SSP1–SSP5) about population, economic growth, inequality and technology that IAM teams use as common starting points for climate scenarios, e.g. SSP2 'middle of the road'.

Running several independent models on the same question with harmonised assumptions. Findings shared across models are considered robust; disagreements show where structure or assumptions drive results.
Searching for very different energy systems whose cost is only slightly above the least-cost optimum. Shows that many system designs cost about the same, so the choice can rest on other criteria.
A modelling assumption that investors know all future costs, demand and policy when they decide. Common in optimisation models; it tends to make transitions look smoother and cheaper than in reality.

Energy in its raw form before conversion: crude oil, coal, gas, uranium, sunlight or wind captured as electricity, biomass. Fossil shares are usually quoted against total primary energy supply. Accounting methods for non-combustible sources differ between publishers, so shares aren't always comparable.
Energy as delivered to end users — electricity, fuels, heat — after conversion and transmission losses. Electrification is usually measured as electricity's share of final energy (about 21% today).

Linking the power sector with heat, transport and industry, e.g. through heat pumps, EVs and electrolysers, so that cheap clean electricity displaces fuels and these loads add flexibility to the grid.

Low-carbon generation that can run whenever needed, for as long as needed — nuclear, geothermal, hydro with reservoirs, gas or biomass with CCS. Studies find that including it lowers the cost of fully decarbonised grids.
The percentage cost drop for each doubling of cumulative production. Solar PV has shown ~20%+ per doubling. Underestimating it is a main reason past outlooks undershot renewables.

Up-front investment to build an asset such as a power plant or grid line, as opposed to operating costs (opex). Nuclear, wind and solar are capex-heavy, so their costs depend strongly on interest rates.
The standard unit for oil demand and supply. The world uses roughly 104 mb/d today.
10¹⁸ joules, the usual unit for national and global energy totals. World primary energy is about 600–650 EJ per year; 1 EJ ≈ 278 TWh.
Uranium enriched to below 20% U-235. Today's light-water reactors use about 3–5%; enrichment between 5% and 20% is called HALEU.
